title: From session agent to always-on agent
lead: The same loop can run per session, survive crashes, or run all the time — each step adds state and responsibility.
cues: Pi: a person at a terminal starts and supervises each run.
Pi Durable: a library for apps whose agents must survive restarts.
Hermes: started by chats and schedules, not only by people.
What grows: state, triggers and the surfaces that reach the agent.
takeaway: Always-on is an architectural decision, not a feature flag.
source: Zechner (2025); Pi docs, github.com/earendil-works/pi · Earendil (2026), Pi Durable, earendil.com/posts/pi-durable · Nous Research, Hermes Agent docs; Alejandro AO (2026), Hermes architecture

title: Pi Durable: surviving a crash
lead: Every step is a task that stores a checkpoint before it moves on.
cues: Checkpoint first: a tool call’s intent is stored before it runs.
After a restart, a new process resumes open tasks.
Replay rule: only tools marked safe rerun; otherwise the model is told.
requestId makes a submission exactly-once.
takeaway: Durability means deciding, per tool, what may happen twice.

title: Hermes: an always-on agent
lead: One agent core, reached through a CLI, chat gateways and editors, and started by a scheduler.
cues: Entry points: CLI, a long-running gateway, ACP clients.
Cron starts work without a person in the loop.
Memory files are always in context; sessions live in SQLite.
Self-improving: the agent writes and patches its own skills.
takeaway: An always-on agent is a service, with a service’s responsibilities.
source: Nous Research, Hermes Agent docs; Alejandro AO (2026), Hermes architecture · Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, §7–10

title: What always-on costs
lead: More autonomy moves risk from the person at the terminal into the architecture.
cues: Each step right adds state that must stay consistent.
Unattended runs need durable checkpoints and replay rules.
Long-running processes fail in new ways: leaks, replays, fragmentation.
Field reports are evidence too: read the issue tracker.
takeaway: Every hour an agent runs unattended is an hour of architecture to own.
source: Zechner (2025); Pi docs, github.com/earendil-works/pi · Earendil (2026), Pi Durable, earendil.com/posts/pi-durable · Hermes issue #5563

title: The platform turn
lead: Harnesses are becoming platforms, and frameworks are becoming harnesses.
cues: Bottom up: model, harness, platform, meta-harness.
Platform: SDKs, durable libraries, ACP servers, skill marketplaces.
Meta-harness: Omnigent ships adapters for 23 harnesses.
Implication: extensions are a supply chain to secure.
takeaway: The developer increasingly programs inside the harness.
source: Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, §14 · Earendil (2026), Pi Durable, earendil.com/posts/pi-durable

title: Recommendations from eleven harnesses
lead: The study ends with 18 recommendations; seven connect directly to today’s topics.
cues: Recommendations come from what eleven systems converged on.
Evidence column: where today’s systems follow or diverge.
R18 splits the field: budgets versus trusting the model to stop.
Use them as defaults, and know when you diverge.
takeaway: Recommendations are evidence, not rules — know when you diverge.
source: Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, §16

title: A minimum viable harness in ~90 lines
lead: The study closes with a scaffold that implements ten of its recommendations.
cues: The while loop is the whole agent.
Limits and compaction run before every model call.
Return when the model stops calling tools.
Left out on purpose: sandbox, multi-agent, MCP, skills.
takeaway: Start minimal; add what your observed failures demand.
source: Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, §16.10, Listing 3
